--- title: "Lab 3: Ordinal Regression" subtitle: "PSY 504: Advanced Statistics" author: "Yeaju Diana Kim" date: today format: html: code-fold: true code-overflow: wrap toc: true toc-depth: 2 execute: message: false warning: false engine: knitr --- ## Instructions - If you are fitting a model, display the model output in a neatly formatted table. (The `tidy()` and `kable()` functions can help!) - If you are creating a plot, use clear labels for all axes, titles, etc. - Commit and push your work to GitHub regularly, at least after each exercise. Write short and informative commit messages. - When you're done, we should be able to knit the final version of the QMD in your GitHub as an HTML. ## Setup ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} library(tidyverse) library(ordinal) library(marginaleffects) library(emmeans) library(car) library(ggeffects) library(knitr) #install.packages('modelsummary') library(modelsummary) library(patchwork) #install.packages('gofcat') library(gofcat) library(sure) library(MASS) options(scipen = 999) ``` ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Part 1: Understanding Thresholds Through Simulation ## The Setup A university has 10 instructors who are **cross-listed** — they each teach one course in the Psychology department and one in Computer Science. At the end of the semester, students in both departments rate these instructors on a 4-point scale: **Poor / Fair / Good / Excellent**. Each instructor has a latent (hidden) "teaching effectiveness" score that we never observe. We only see the ordinal rating. Now, **both departments evaluate the same instructors**, but their evaluation forms use **different descriptions** for the rating categories. **Psychology's form:** - Poor = "Did not meet basic expectations" - Fair = "Meets minimum expectations" - Good = "Consistently above average" - Excellent = "Outstanding in all respects" **Computer Science's form:** - Poor = "Did not meet basic expectations" - Fair = "Meets minimum expectations" - Good = "Solid and competent" - Excellent = "Solid and competent, with minor distinction" Notice that in CS, students have to split hairs between "Good" and "Excellent" as the descriptions barely differ. This compresses the top two categories together. Consequently almost everyone who would be "Good" in Psychology ends up rated "Excellent" in CS, not because the teaching improved, but because the **scale changed**. Here's the simulation code. **Read it carefully before running it.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} set.seed(504) # 10 cross-listed instructors with latent teaching effectiveness instructors <- tibble( id = 1:10, effectiveness = rnorm(10, mean = 0, sd = 1.2) ) # Each instructor rated by 20 students per department ratings_latent <- instructors %>% rowwise() %>% mutate(latent = list(rnorm(20, mean = effectiveness, sd = 1))) %>% unnest(latent) %>% ungroup() # --- THREE THRESHOLDS PRODUCE FOUR CATEGORIES --- # Psychology: balanced scale tau_psych <- c(-1.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Computer Science: compressed top end tau_cs <- c(-1.0, 0.0, 0.3) ratings <- ratings_latent %>% mutate( eval_psych = case_when( latent <= tau_psych[1] ~ "Poor", latent <= tau_psych[2] ~ "Fair", latent <= tau_psych[3] ~ "Good", TRUE ~ "Excellent" ), eval_psych = ordered(eval_psych, levels = c("Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent")), eval_cs = case_when( latent <= tau_cs[1] ~ "Poor", latent <= tau_cs[2] ~ "Fair", latent <= tau_cs[3] ~ "Good", TRUE ~ "Excellent" ), eval_cs = ordered(eval_cs, levels = c("Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent")) ) ``` ::: ### Question 1.1: Visualize the latent distribution {.unnumbered} Create a density plot of the latent scores with vertical dashed lines for Psychology's thresholds ($\tau_1 = -1$, $\tau_2 = 0$, $\tau_3 = 1$). Label the four regions (Poor, Fair, Good, Excellent) on the plot. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint: Key geoms"} `geom_density()` for the curve, `geom_vline(xintercept = ...)` for the thresholds (use `linetype = "dashed"`), and `annotate("text", x = ..., y = ..., label = ...)` to place category labels in each region. You'll need one `annotate()` call per label. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(ratings_latent, aes(x = latent)) + geom_density() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 0, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") + annotate("text", x = -2, y = 0.2, label = "Poor") + annotate("text", x = -0.5, y = 0.2, label = "Fair") + annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.2, label = "Good") + annotate("text", x = 2, y = 0.2, label = "Excellent") + labs(title = "Latent Teaching Effectiveness Distribution", x = "Teaching Effectiveness", y = "Density") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Lab3_ordinal-regression_DianaKim_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Question 1.2: Identical instructors, different scales {.unnumbered} Create side-by-side stacked bar charts showing the observed rating distributions for Psychology and CS. The instructors didn't change, so what did? What does this tell you about what thresholds control? How the instructors are rated by the students changed. Different thresholds can cause different categorization based on how you rate the samples, even when latent variables are the same. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint: Data wrangling"} First, create a frequency table for each department using `count()`, rename the rating column to a shared name like `category`, and add a `dept` label column. Then `bind_rows()` them together. Compute proportions with `mutate(prop = n / sum(n))` grouped by department. Plot with `geom_col(position = "stack")` mapping `x = dept`, `y = prop`, and `fill = category`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} psych_table <- ratings %>% count(eval_psych) %>% rename(category = eval_psych) %>% mutate(dept = "Psychology") cs_table <- ratings %>% count(eval_cs) %>% rename(category = eval_cs) %>% mutate(dept = "Computer Science") both_table <- bind_rows(psych_table, cs_table) %>% group_by(dept) %>% mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup() ggplot(both_table, aes(x = dept, y = prop, fill = category)) + geom_col(position = "stack") + labs(title = "Rating Distributions In Departments", x = "Department", y = "Proportion", fill = "Rating" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Lab3_ordinal-regression_DianaKim_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Exercise 1.3: What does tau live on? {.unnumbered} The thresholds $\tau_1 = -1$, $\tau_2 = 0$, $\tau_3 = 1$ are on the latent "teaching effectiveness" scale — the continuous axis you generated but would never observe in real data. The model re-expresses these same cut points as **log-cumulative-odds** — a transformation of the latent scale that makes the math linear. Convert between them: a) Convert the Psychology Dept thresholds to cumulative probabilities using `plogis()`. What does each value mean? Thresholds for cumulative probabilities of rating categories (e.g., good, excellent). ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint: What does plogis() do?"} `plogis()` is the inverse logit. It converts log-cumulative-odds back to a probability: $\text{plogis}(\tau) = \frac{e^\tau}{1 + e^\tau} = P(Y \leq k)$ ::: b) Suppose you want a rating distribution where 10% are Poor, 30% Fair, 40% Good, and 20% Excellent. What thresholds would produce this? Use `qlogis()`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint: What does qlogis() do?"} `qlogis()` is the logit function, which goes the other direction. Give it a cumulative probability and it returns the threshold: $\text{qlogis}(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p} = \tau$ ::: ::: panel-tabset ## Your turn ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # (a) Thresholds to cumulative probabilities thresholds <- c(-1.0, 0.0, 1.0) cumul_probs <- plogis(thresholds) cumul_probs # Then get category-specific probabilities cat_probs <- diff(c(0, cumul_probs, 1)) cat_probs # (b) Desired split to thresholds desired_split <- c(0.10, 0.30, 0.40, 0.20) cumul_desired <- cumsum(desired_split[1:3]) # which elements? cumul_desired needed_thresholds <- qlogis(cumul_desired) needed_thresholds ``` ::: ## Expected output (a) Cumulative probs: 0.269, 0.500, 0.731 Category probs: 0.269, 0.231, 0.231, 0.269 (b) Cumulative at cuts: 0.10, 0.40, 0.80 Required thresholds: -2.197, -0.405, 1.386 ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Part 2: Manual Calculation — From Counts to Log-Cumulative-Odds The goal of this section is to **demystify model output**. When you later see `Poor|Fair = -1.23` in a `clm()` summary, you'll think: "that's the log-cumulative-odds I already computed by hand." ### Exercise 2.1: Build the table {.unnumbered} Using Psychology Dept's ratings, compute the following for each category: the count, proportion, cumulative proportion, cumulative odds, and log-cumulative-odds. Display the result as a table using `kable()`. ::: panel-tabset ## Your turn ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hand_calc <- ratings %>% count(eval_psych) %>% ##? rename(category = eval_psych) %>% mutate( proportion = n / sum(n), cumul_proportion = cumsum(proportion), cumul_odds = cumul_proportion / (1 - cumul_proportion), log_cumul_odds = log(cumul_odds) ) hand_calc %>% kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: ## Hint: What's cumulative odds? Cumulative odds = $\frac{P(Y \leq k)}{P(Y > k)} = \frac{\text{cum\_proportion}}{1 - \text{cum\_proportion}}$ Then take `log()` (natural log, not log10). The last category (Excellent) will be `Inf`. This is because $P(Y \leq \text{Excellent}) = 1$, so the odds are $1/0 = \infty$. ::: ### Question 2.2: Compare to model output {.unnumbered} Fit an intercept-only ordinal model on the Psychology Dept data: `clm(eval_psych ~ 1, data = ratings)`. Compare the model's threshold estimates to your hand-calculated log-cumulative-odds. How do they compare, and what does this tell you about what the model is doing? They're identical! The model is estimating cumulative probabilities and reporting log-cumulative odds. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} intercept_only <- clm(eval_psych ~ 1, data = ratings) modelsummary(intercept_only) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

It visualizes the numbers you computed in Exercise 2.1, with gray bars showing cumulative probabilities and blue segments showing category-specific probabilities. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} freq_table <- ratings %>% count(eval_psych) %>% rename(category = eval_psych) %>% mutate( prop = n / sum(n), cumul_prop = cumsum(prop), cumul_prop_lag = lag(cumul_prop, default = 0) ) ggplot(freq_table) + geom_col(aes(x = category, y = cumul_prop), fill = "gray70", width = 0.5) + geom_segment(aes(x = as.numeric(category) + 0.15, xend = as.numeric(category) + 0.15, y = cumul_prop_lag, yend = cumul_prop), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 3) + geom_text(aes(x = as.numeric(category) + 0.3, y = (cumul_prop + cumul_prop_lag) / 2, label = round(prop, 2)), color = "steelblue", size = 5, fontface = "bold") + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) + labs( title = "Cumulative vs. category-specific probabilities", subtitle = "Gray = cumulative P(Y ≤ k) Blue = category P(Y = k)", x = "Rating", y = "Probability" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 14) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Lab3_ordinal-regression_DianaKim_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Answer these questions: What do the gray bar and blue segment for "Fair" represent? Write them as probability statements. The gray bar shows a cumulative probability of 'Fair' and below 'Fair' categories. There is 38% probability that the ratings will fall into 'Fair' or 'Poor' category. The blue bar, on the other hand, shows category-specific probability. There's 26% probability that the ratings fall into 'Fair' category alone. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Part 3: Conceptual Questions ### Question 3.1 {.unnumbered} How does the **cumulative logit** link function differ from the ordinary logit link used in binary logistic regression? The cumulative logit is: $\log\frac{P(Y \leq k)}{P(Y > k)}$ For an outcome with $K$ categories, how many equations does this produce? Answer in 2--3 sentences. In binary logistic regression, the logit link models a single equation because there are only two categories. In a cumulative logit model, it models cumulative probabilities. For an outcome with k categories, it produced k-1 equations. ### Question 3.2: Why not just use linear regression (aka metric models)? {.unnumbered} Linear regression, ANOVA, and t-tests are all metric models. Metric models assume the numbers you assign to categories have equal spacing and meaningful distances, where you're treating your scale like a ruler with evenly spaced tick marks. Using the simulation data, code Psychology Dept ratings as numbers: Poor = 1, Fair = 2, Good = 3, Excellent = 4. Fit `lm(rating_numeric ~ effectiveness)`. Then recode as Poor = 1, Fair = 2, Good = 3, Excellent = 10. Fit the model again. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ratings_1 <- ratings %>% mutate(rating_numeric = as.numeric(eval_psych)) model1 <- lm(rating_numeric ~ effectiveness, data = ratings_1) modelsummary(model1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

In one sentence, explain why they differ and what this reveals about metric models. The slope of the first model (1,2,3,4) is 0.452 while the second model (1,2,3,10)'s slope is 1.706. Changing the numeric scales can affect the interpretation of ordinal outcomes. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Part 4: Modeling the GBBO Data The data comes from the Great British Bake Off (GBBO). In each episode, bakers face a "technical challenge" where they receive a recipe with minimal instructions and are judged blind. The judges rank every baker from best to worst. We will focus on the **top 3 finishers**. Rank is ordinal, as 1st is better than 2nd and 2nd is better than 3rd, but we cannot say the gap between 1st and 2nd equals the gap between 2nd and 3rd. This is the kind of data that ordinal regression is suited for. Do Gender and Age predict how bakers rank in the technical? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} gbbo <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/suyoghc/PSY-504_Spring-2025/refs/heads/main/Ordinal%20Regression/data/GBBO.csv") ``` ::: ### Exercise 4.1: Prepare the data {.unnumbered} Filter to only top 3 ranks. Convert `Rank` to an ordered factor (1 = best, so think about the ordering). Convert `Gender` to a factor. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint: Factor ordering"} The column is called `Technical Rank` (with a space), so rename it first with `rename(Rank = \`Technical Rank\`)\`. What does "higher" mean here? Rank 1 is best. You need to decide whether your ordered factor goes 1 \< 2 \< 3 (best to worst) or 3 \< 2 \< 1 (worst to best). The model interprets higher factor levels as "more" of the outcome. Think about what direction makes sense for your interpretation. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} gb <- gbbo %>% rename(Rank = `Technical Rank`) %>% # fix column name filter(Rank %in% c(1, 2, 3)) %>% drop_na() %>% mutate( Rank = ordered(Rank, levels = c(3, 2, 1)), # 3 < 2 < 1, so "higher" = better rank Gender = factor(Gender) ) head(gb) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 3 Gender Age Rank 1 F 30 2 2 M 31 3 3 M 24 1 4 F 45 2 5 M 25 1 6 F 37 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} table(gb$Rank) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 3 2 1 102 104 103 ``` ::: ::: ### Question 4.2: Explore {.unnumbered} Create two visualizations: a) A bar chart showing the proportion of bakers in each rank by Gender. b) A bar chart showing the proportion of bakers in each rank by Age (bin Age into groups using `cut()`). ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint: Proportional bar charts"} `geom_bar(position = "fill")` gives proportions instead of counts. Map `x = Gender` (or your age groups) and `fill = Rank`. For part (b), create age bins with something like `cut(Age, breaks = c(15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 75))` inside a `mutate()` before plotting. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #a ggplot(gb, aes(x = Gender, fill = Rank)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) + labs( title = "Proportion by Gender", x = "Gender", y = "Proportion" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 14) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Lab3_ordinal-regression_DianaKim_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #b gb_age <- gb %>% mutate(AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 75))) ggplot(gb_age, aes(x = AgeGroup, fill = Rank)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) + labs( title = "Proportion by Age group", x = "Age group", y = "Proportion" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Lab3_ordinal-regression_DianaKim_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-2.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Question 4.3: Build models {.unnumbered} Fit the following models using `clm()` from the `ordinal` package: - **Model 0:** Intercept only — `Rank ~ 1` - **Model 1:** `Rank ~ Gender` - **Model 2:** `Rank ~ Gender + Age` - **Model 3:** `Rank ~ Gender * Age` For Model 2: a) Report the threshold estimates. What do they represent? 3\|2 is -0.6005 (log-odds of rank being third place) and 2\|1 is 0.8048 (log-odds of rank being third or second place). b) Exponentiate the coefficients. Interpret the odds ratio for `Age` in one sentence. When age increases 1 year, the odds of being in a higher rank increase 1.0056%(?). c) Using Model 2, what is the predicted probability of Rank 1 for a 30-year-old female? Use `predictions()` from the `marginaleffects` package. 34.6%. Have we learned how to use this function..? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint: Interpreting thresholds"} The thresholds are the log-cumulative-odds of $P(Y \leq k)$ when all predictors are zero. They define the baseline distribution — where the cuts fall before any predictor shifts the distribution. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} m0 <- clm(Rank ~ 1, data = gb) m1 <- clm(Rank ~ Gender, data = gb) m2 <- clm(Rank ~ Gender + Age, data = gb) m3 <- clm(Rank ~ Gender * Age, data = gb) summary(m2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` formula: Rank ~ Gender + Age data: gb link threshold nobs logLik AIC niter max.grad cond.H logit flexible 309 -338.86 685.72 3(0) 1.05e-10 2.9e+04 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Is the interaction warranted? Yes. Model 3 is significantly better than Model 2. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint: What is anova() doing here?"} Each model's parameters are estimated by maximizing its likelihood function, finding the parameter values that make the observed data as probable as possible. `anova()` performs a likelihood ratio test. It computes: $$LR = -2 \log\left(\frac{L_{\text{simple}}}{L_{\text{complex}}}\right)$$ This statistic follows a chi-square distribution. A significant p-value means the complex model fits meaningfully better, so the interaction is worth keeping. A non-significant p-value means the extra parameters aren't earning their keep, so you should prefer the simpler model. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m2, m3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Likelihood ratio tests of cumulative link models: formula: link: threshold: m2 Rank ~ Gender + Age logit flexible m3 Rank ~ Gender * Age logit flexible no.par AIC logLik LR.stat df Pr(>Chisq) m2 4 685.72 -338.86 m3 5 683.28 -336.64 4.437 1 0.03517 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: ### Question 5.2 {.unnumbered} Create a publication-quality comparison table of all four models using `modelsummary()`. In OLS, the slope *is* the marginal effect, because one unit of X always produces β units of change in Y. That's because the model predicts Y directly, with no transformation. In any GLM with a nonlinear link (logistic regression, Poisson, ordinal, ...), the slope and the marginal effect come apart. The model estimates β on a transformed scale (log-odds, log-counts), but the relationship between that scale and probability is a curve, not a line. The same β of 0.5 might shift a probability from 0.10 to 0.15 (a 5-point change) near the tails, but from 0.45 to 0.57 (a 12-point change) near the middle. The coefficient is identical in both cases, but its impact differs because the curve is steepest in the center and flat at the extremes. For ordinal regression specifically, there's an added wrinkle: the marginal effect is different for **each category**. Age might increase P(Rank 1) while simultaneously decreasing P(Rank 3), because probability must redistribute. `avg_comparisons()` handles all of this. It computes the probability-scale effect at every observation, then averages — giving you one summary per category in percentage points. Here's a worked example interpreting the effect of Gender: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} avg_comparisons(m2, variables = "Gender", type = "prob") %>% kable(digits = 3, caption = "Average marginal effect of Gender on each rank") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Average marginal effect of Gender on each rank |term |group |contrast | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| s.value| conf.low| conf.high| |:------|:-----|:--------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:|-------:|--------:|---------:| |Gender |3 |M - F | 0.042| 0.047| 0.904| 0.366| 1.451| -0.049| 0.134| |Gender |2 |M - F | 0.000| 0.003| -0.035| 0.972| 0.040| -0.006| 0.006| |Gender |1 |M - F | -0.042| 0.046| -0.911| 0.362| 1.464| -0.133| 0.049| ::: ::: **Interpretation example:** *"Switching from female to male changes the probability of achieving Rank 1 by -4.2 percentage points, on average.
